doc.title: Christine Jensen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 4, 2024

title: Replacing Bill Dobbins and the future of jazz education
summary: Jensen says she replaces Bill Dobbins and expects inclusion to grow as the first generation of jazz professors retires; jazz in institutions still sits in classical space.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I heard there was a lot of applicants and I am replacing someone who is irreplaceable in the name of Bill Dobbins, who has left a legacy in so many ways. Why did they hire me? I can never get into that too much. I do feel this music and the movement of it is in for a big change especially within the institution walls of the young business of teaching jazz at the higher level, which only started fifty years ago or so. And there was a lot of tenure involved and there still is, but that generation is now starting to retire so I think we’re going to see a lot more inclusion — best way I can put it — with where the music is going and where the education of the music is going.

It’s become a large business as well. I remember, I was at SUNY Fredonia and I graduated in ’72 and we had a fine jazz band but there were no classes, there were no jazz professors, there was a struggle to get rehearsal rooms for jazz etcetera, and think of where it’s at now.

We still have a ways to go though. I’m deep in thought of all of what you’re talking about partly because I’m teaching a master’s pedagogy in jazz course which we discuss a lot of these things and jazz in the institution has blossomed out of the classical institution, therefore they’ve held the reins and had all the rules and had all the space. And they have let us come into their space a little bit. And it hasn’t been the other way around ever. So what you’re describing is what I feel still.
